Do deep web research on modern thought leadership around measuring software engineering productivity, effectiveness, and INDIVIDUAL engineer impact. I am building an "engineering impact" scoring model from GitHub data and need to ground it in what credible practitioners and researchers actually argue in 2024-2026.

Research and synthesize these specific threads:

1. **DORA metrics** (deployment frequency, lead time for change, change failure rate, time to restore) — what they measure, and critically the well-known caveat that they are TEAM/system metrics and explicitly NOT for individual evaluation. Get the current state (DORA 2024/2025 reports, any AI-related findings).

2. **The SPACE framework** (Forsgren, Storey, Nagappan, et al.) — Satisfaction, Performance, Activity, Communication/Collaboration, Efficiency/Flow. What it says about why single metrics fail and why you need multiple dimensions across different levels.

3. **DX Core 4** (Laura Tacho / Abi Noda / DX) — the newer unified framework (speed, effectiveness, quality, business impact) and the "Developer Experience Index". What they say about individual-level measurement — I believe they have a specific stance on when it IS and ISN'T appropriate.

4. **Critiques of individual developer metrics** — the case against LOC, commit counts, story points, "10x engineer" measurement. Goodhart's Law in engineering orgs. What specifically goes wrong. Look for named practitioners: Kent Beck, Gergely Orosz (Pragmatic Engineer), Will Larson (Staff Eng / Irrational Exuberance), Charity Majors, Abi Noda, Laura Tacho, Martin Fowler / Thoughtworks.

5. **What people argue DOES capture real individual impact** — specifically look for arguments about: code review as leverage/multiplier work, mentorship and unblocking others, "glue work" (Tanya Reilly's essay), reducing bus factor vs creating silos, blast radius / criticality of code touched, reliability and rework/churn rates, cross-team breadth, the distinction between an engineer's output vs their effect on the team's output. Also look for the "Staff engineer archetypes" (Will Larson: Tech Lead, Architect, Solver, Right Hand) as a framing for different KINDS of impact.

6. **Code churn / rework rate** as a quality signal (work that gets rewritten or reverted shortly after being merged) — who advocates for it, what the thresholds/caveats are.

7. Anything credible on **measuring open-source maintainer impact** specifically — since my target repo is an open-source company (PostHog), where engaging external contributors is real work that never shows up in commit counts.

Deliverable: a synthesized brief, not a link dump. For each thread give me the core claim, who argues it, and — most importantly — the CONCRETE IMPLICATION for someone designing a multi-dimensional individual impact score from GitHub data. Explicitly flag the strongest arguments AGAINST what I'm doing, because I want to address them head-on rather than pretend they don't exist. Include specific quotable lines or stats where they're strong, with attribution. Cite URLs for the key sources.

I've found comprehensive search results on this topic. Here's what the research shows about Goodhart's Law and its application to engineering metrics and individual developer productivity:

## Core Concept

Goodhart's Law states: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." When a metric becomes the primary target, people tend to manipulate it, making it a poor measure of real success.

## Gaming Behaviors in Developer Productivity

The critique is particularly sharp when metrics are used for individual performance evaluation. Developers game the system, split PRs artificially, inflate story points, and focus on metrics over value. Specific examples include:

- **Story Points**: Developers inflate story point estimates to appear more productive.
- **Pull Requests**: When PRs merged per sprint becomes a target, developers split every feature into 5-7 micro-PRs where each one is technically mergeable but makes no sense in isolation, and code review becomes a joke because reviewers can't understand context across 6 PRs.
- **Code Quantity**: When lines of code becomes a target, developers write more code than necessary—functions that could be one-liners become twenty.

## Structural Problem with All Metrics

The critique runs deeper than just bad metric choices. Every productivity metric — from lines of code to DORA — measures a proxy for value, and every proxy is subject to Goodhart's Law once it becomes a target. Replacing one metric with a better one does not escape this problem; it only delays it.

## Recommended Approach

To avoid the negative impacts of Goodhart's Law, you need to track the right metrics and adopt a mindset that prioritizes actual outcomes over vanity numbers, focusing on team performance, product quality, and long-term success instead of individual output.

## Core Concept

Goodhart's Law states: "Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes." When a metric becomes the primary target, people tend to manipulate it, making it a poor measure of real success.

- **Pull Requests**: When PRs merged per sprint becomes a target, developers split every feature into 5-7 micro-PRs where each one is technically mergeable but makes no sense in isolation, and code review becomes a joke because reviewers can't understand context across 6 PRs.

The critique runs deeper than just bad metric choices. Every productivity metric — from lines of code to DORA — measures a proxy for value, and every proxy is subject to Goodhart's Law once it becomes a target. Replacing one metric with a better one does not escape this problem; it only delays it.

# Core Arguments from Part 2: Beck & Orosz on Developer Productivity

## Primary Thesis
The authors argue that measuring developer productivity through rigid frameworks—as McKinsey proposes—causes more organizational harm than benefit through unintended behavior changes and culture degradation.

## Key Arguments Against Measurement Frameworks

**On Gaming Systems:**
- "Individual goals discourages people from working together, as everyone is chasing their own quota" (Beck, discussing sales)
- When a "rockstar" recruiter was measured solely on placements, they made false verbal promises to candidates, creating months of cleanup work

**On Team vs. Individual Performance:**
The article emphasizes: "Individual performance does not directly predict team performance." They cite sports examples (Greece's Euro 2004 soccer victory with the 15th-ranked team) to show teams with average players can outperform star-laden squads.

## The Measurement Hierarchy They Propose

Instead of effort/output metrics, prioritize:
1. **Impact** (revenue, cost reduction, business metrics)
2. **System performance** (speed, reliability)
3. **Developer effectiveness** (speed, ease, quality, satisfaction)

Their framework ranks what to measure:
- **Avoid measuring:** effort and output as performance incentives
- **Primary focus:** team outcomes and impact
- **Secondary debugging:** effort/output data only when outcomes underperform

## Goodhart's Law Application

"When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." They illustrate this with a Scrum team where story-point velocity became the goal, causing engineers to inflate estimates and include low-value high-point tasks.

## Alternative Approach to "Good Measurement"

High-performing teams demonstrate:
- Impact aligned with or exceeding expectations
- Efficient execution appropriate to team context
- Hands-on leadership that spots and addresses issues promptly

The authors note: "Running a high-performing team is a hands-on approach," suggesting direct observation beats metrics.

## What They Reject

They reject measuring:
- Individual pull request counts
- Lines of code
- Sprint velocity as success indicator
- Granular individual contribution attribution

## On Measurement's Hidden Cost

The central warning: measurement inevitably shapes behavior. "The more you measure, the more you shape the culture and how people work." They acknowledge measurement is impossible without impact, stating consultants claiming otherwise are misleading.

# Martin Fowler's Argument on Measuring Productivity

## The Core Problem

Fowler establishes that measuring productivity is fundamentally impossible because **"we can't measure output"** in software development. He defines productivity as requiring measurement of both input and output, but argues the industry lacks the ability to quantify what software development actually produces.

## On Lines of Code (LOC)

Fowler is particularly critical of LOC as a productivity metric:

> "Any good developer knows that they can code the same stuff with huge variations in lines of code"

He emphasizes that well-designed code tends to be shorter due to eliminating duplication, while "Copy and paste programming leads to high LOC counts and poor design." His key insight: even if one developer writes 100,000 LOC and another writes 10,000 LOC for the same system in equal time, this doesn't indicate the first is more productive—rather, it suggests poorer design.

## On Function Points

While Fowler shows "a little more sympathy" for Function Points, he remains skeptical. He cites stories where "a single system getting counts that varied by a factor of three from different function point counters."

More fundamentally, he argues that even accurate functionality measurement misses true productivity: delivering 100 function points of marginally useful features is less productive than delivering 50 function points that customers actually need.

## Output vs. Outcome: The Business Value Standard

Fowler's central thesis distinguishes between direct output and true productivity:

> "true output is something else" beyond mere functionality delivered

He argues **true productivity must be based on delivered business value**. His example: if one developer's work generates $5 million in profit while another's generates $10 million from fewer features, the second developer demonstrates superior productivity.

Fowler extends this to project success rates, noting that success metrics focusing on completion rates miss the actual value created, which may take years to materialize.

However, the study was measuring individual programmers doing isolated coding tasks in a controlled environment, not engineers working on real systems in real teams over real timeframes.

## Key Problems with the Myth

10x refers to the difference between the best and worst developers, not the best and average. More importantly, in a controlled environment, the variation between most software engineers is much more modest. There is also a significant variation in how the same person performs across multiple tasks. A person who outperforms others in some task may be average in another.

## What the Research Actually Shows

The 10x engineer was always a simplification. It compressed something real (variance in individual capability) into a framework that drew the wrong conclusions from it. Additionally, the 10x measurement is about execution velocity on isolated tasks. It says nothing about judgment, architecture, mentoring, communication, or any of the other things that make engineers valuable.

## The Team Impact Problem

Critically, the most important metric was the team's productivity. And this was best increased with soft skills, such as better communications and decision making. Research shows individual technical prowess doesn't translate to team success—in some cases, high-output individuals can create negative team dynamics and technical debt.

## What She Says is ILLEGITIMATE:

**Direct metrics to avoid:**
- "lines of code, story points completed, or deployment frequency are not appropriate to measure individual performance"

- "A fast way to reassure your team that you don't understand their job is to pick what they perceive as arbitrary and unfair metrics"
- Risk of gaming: "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure"

**Her core principle:**
"Instead of looking for a list of metrics to determine how you measure performance, figure out how you want to measure performance and then find metrics that help you measure the stuff that's important to your company."

"Focus on outcomes, not output, but you might use output metrics like activity from GitHub and JIRA to debug why outcomes were missed."

**Exception to the rule:**
"using team metrics to measure individual performance is generally unfair *unless* it's the explicit role of the individual to influence the system performance metrics" (staff+ and management roles)

# Summary of "No Silver Bullets: Why Understanding Software Cycle Time is Messy, Not Magic"

## Authors & Dataset
**Authors:** John C. Flournoy, Carol S. Lee, Maggie Wu, Catherine M. Hicks

**Dataset:** Over 55,000 observations across 216 organizations

## Method
The researchers employed Bayesian hierarchical modeling to analyze cycle time (the metric measuring time from ticket creation to completion). This approach appropriately separated individual-level variation from organizational-level variation.

## Key Findings

**Predictive Factors:** The analysis identified modest associations with cycle time, including:
- Coding days per week
- Number of merged pull requests
- Degree of collaboration

However, these effects were modest in magnitude.

**Variance Explanation:** The critical finding concerns unexplained variation. The abstract notes: "these effects are set against considerable unexplained variation both between and within individuals."

## Conclusions on Individual/Team Evaluation

The authors emphasize a crucial limitation for performance management: "any single observation provides limited signal about typical performance." 

They advocate for a systems-level approach, concluding that "improving software delivery velocity likely requires systems-level thinking rather than individual-focused interventions."

This research directly challenges using cycle time metrics as a basis for evaluating individual developers, demonstrating that substantial unexplained variation undermines such assessments.

# Swarmia's Position on Individual-Level Developer Metrics

## Should NEVER Be Measured at Individual Level

Swarmia explicitly warns against using metrics to evaluate individuals, stating: "Using arbitrary metrics (as in, metrics alone) to evaluate individuals. Commits per day, PRs merged, lines of code written — these numbers are easy to collect but they almost always measure the wrong thing."

They provide a concrete example: "The engineer who spends a day helping three teammates get unstuck has contributed enormously, but their commit count is zero (and so what?)."

## Acceptable Individual Context (Not Performance Targets)

Swarmia accepts individual-level *visibility* into:
- AI tool usage by person (for cost tracking, not productivity assessment)
- Time spent in different work categories
- Individual contribution to aggregate metrics (for context, not judgment)

However, they emphasize: "Don't set a target" on metrics like AI adoption rates per person.

## Key Verbatim Quotes on This Issue

- "The engineer who writes a thousand lines of code that creates technical debt for years shows up great on some activity metrics."
- "An engineer with low AI usage might be working on the system nobody wants an agent anywhere near."

## Recommended Metric Set

Swarmia's 20 essential metrics focus on **organizational and team-level** measurement:

1. AI cost by tool/team
2. Cost per unit of output
3. Active use and idle licenses
4-5. AI-assisted PR share and flow metrics
6-7. Agent work and review metrics
8. Quality on AI-assisted work
9-13. DORA metrics (5 total)
14-17. Cycle time, batch size, review time, CI speed
18-20. Investment balance, planning accuracy, developer surveys

# The Flawed Five Engineering Productivity Metrics

**Author:** Abi Noda (published March 30, 2021)

## The Five Metrics and Arguments Against Them:

### 1. **Commits**
**Argument:** Commit counts reveal nothing about work value or quality and are easily gamed. As Jaana Dogan noted: "Number of commits don't tell anything about the value and quality of those commits."

### 2. **Lines of Code**
**Argument:** Different languages generate vastly different line counts for identical functionality. Refactoring—a positive practice—reduces code. Scott Hanselman stated: "Number of lines of code written is not a measure of your value to a project."

### 3. **Pull Request Count**
**Argument:** Counting PRs ignores size, effort, and impact while incentivizing unnecessary fragmentation. Noda cites GitLab's OKR targeting a 20% increase in merge requests per engineer as an example of flawed practice.

### 4. **Velocity Points**
**Argument:** Using points to measure productivity incentivizes estimate inflation, destroying their original purpose. Allen Holub observed: "Jira tracks individual 'productivity' using points per Sprint, thereby destroying the careers of highly productive people."

### 5. **'Impact'**
**Argument:** This proprietary metric repackages lines-of-code problems with added complexity and misleading nomenclature that enables managerial misuse.

# Kent Beck's Position on Developer Productivity Metrics

## Core Argument

Kent maintains cautious skepticism about metrics, grounded in concern about systemic abuse. He frames the discussion around **Goodhart's Law** as non-negotiable: "When you pitch metrics, it's in your best interest that people adopt them. How do you navigate both communicating the upside and the potential downside?"

## His Key Concerns

**Misalignment with reality:** Many developers lack exposure to genuinely efficient environments. He states: "How many developers have actually experienced a really effective development environment? Do they know what really good looks like?"

**Communication risk:** There's persistent danger that metrics messaging becomes "We need you to hurry up," which programmers detect regardless of intent.

**Surveillance dangers:** He expresses broader worry: "Look at the shift in the political climate toward the surveillance economy - that's the societal direction we're going. For creative work, that's a disaster."

## The Problem with Traditional Metrics

Raw commit counts reward gaming, not delivery, and measuring lines of code or commit count as a proxy for AI impact can inflate volume without increasing delivered value—a 3x increase in code volume does not equal a 3x increase in productivity.

Claims often count suggestions accepted, not whether the code was modified, deleted, or ever made it to production, making them largely meaningless for benchmarking.

## Attribution Challenges with AI Agents

Heuristic and watermark detection, which most tools use when attempting AI attribution without client-level capture, reaches only about 20–25% accuracy and produces noisy signals from pattern matching and code style analysis. ## Structural Recommendations

Best practice is to never measure individual engineers but measure the team or the system, and engineers should see the data first and set improvement targets. Raw commit counts, PR volume, and ticket close rates divorced from outcome data create a measurement system that is easy to game and meaningless to improve.

- Develop independent technical judgment to evaluate contributions fairly

# Gergely Orosz on Measuring Individual Developer Productivity

## His Core Argument Against Individual Metrics

Orosz contends that individual developer productivity cannot be meaningfully measured. He notes: **"Any single metric you give to people, it can - and will - be gamed."** Examples include lines of code (encourages busywork), closed tickets (leads to gaming the system), and commit frequency (results in artificial fragmentation).

He asks pointedly: **"If developer productivity can be measured, how is there not a single standard of measuring this in the industry?"** This rhetorical question underscores the fundamental impossibility of the endeavor.

## The Context Exception: Manager Assessment

Orosz acknowledges one legitimate form of individual assessment—when conducted **by engineering managers with proper context**. Managers can observe metrics like code review turnaround, commit patterns, and mentorship contributions, but only if they dig deeper to understand circumstances. He emphasizes: **"There's a wealth of data to look at: but none of it is useful without context."**

For example, reduced commits might indicate mentoring work rather than laziness.

## His Recommendation: Competency Frameworks

Instead of individual metrics, Orosz advocates using **structured competency frameworks tied to career levels**. Top tech companies establish clear expectations for each engineering level and provide ongoing feedback against those competencies during performance reviews, rather than relying on quantitative data points.

## SPACE Framework and Individual-Level Metrics

The SPACE framework was led by Nicole Forsgren, a member of the DORA team and co-author of the book Accelerate. According to the SPACE of Developer Productivity paper, "Activity metrics alone do not reveal which of these is the case, so they should never be used in isolation", referring to the various reasons why activity levels may increase.

More broadly, the authors developed SPACE to dispel persisting myths about developer productivity, such as the idea that productivity is about activity volume, tools, or individual performance. Direct attribution of business outcomes to individual developer work is often impossible, which represents a fundamental caveat about individual-level measurement.

The framework emphasizes a multi-dimensional approach: the researchers suggest distinct metrics that apply to individual-, team-, and system-levels, and importantly, SPACE does not advocate for using all metrics at once, rather to carefully select a reduced set that spans across all three levels and captures different productivity dimensions.

# Research on Measuring Developer Activity

## What Research Does NOT Support

**Individual activity metrics are fundamentally flawed** because they capture only a narrow slice of developer work. Google researchers note that "lines of code per minute will not tell you which software developers are the best" – unlike measuring physical output, more code doesn't equal better engineering.

The SPACE framework authors specifically caution against individual metrics. Dr. Margaret-Anne Storey stated: "I often see companies focusing on metrics like the number of pull requests, which we do not recommend."

## Key Pitfalls of Individual-Level Measurement

**Gaming and morale damage:** Developers fear measurement systems and may "commit unnecessary code just to increase LOC ratings" for self-preservation. Google researchers found that tracking individual performance "could bring down overall productivity" and damage employee morale and retention.

**Limited practical value:** Managers typically "already know who the low performers are," making metrics redundant. Activity metrics cannot identify high performers, help developers grow skills, or reveal actual productivity bottlenecks—higher activity may indicate either inefficiency or better tools.

## What Research Recommends Instead

Focus on organizational factors enabling effectiveness rather than individual output. Improved performance review processes and role clarity matter more than activity metrics for developing talent and improving productivity.

content.content:
# Sean Goedecke's Counter-Argument on Glue Work

Goedecke argues that glue work **should not be systematically rewarded** because companies deliberately discourage it. His reasoning is pragmatic rather than callous:

**His Core Claim:**
Companies don't reward glue work "because they don't want you prioritizing it" — they want engineers shipping features instead. He contends that "Your job is to execute the mission of your company's leadership," not to self-select improvement projects.

**Key Verbatim Quotes:**
- "It is better to execute that mission at 60% efficiency than to spend all your time increasing efficiency in general"
- "you should do glue work _tactically_...for the projects you lead...You won't be rewarded for the glue work specifically, but you will be rewarded for the success of the project"

**His Position:**
Goedecke doesn't think glue work is bad—he thinks **selective, project-focused glue work is smart career strategy**. But doing it broadly across teams burns engineers out and creates unsustainable dependencies on exceptional individuals. The solution isn't rewarding all glue work; it's being strategic about when to do it.

He frames this as realistic organizational psychology, not cynicism.

# Will Larson's Four Staff Engineer Archetypes

## Tech Lead
**Definition:** Guides the approach and execution of a particular team or cluster of teams, partnering closely with one or more managers.

**Work & Impact:** Tech Leads scope complex tasks, coordinate team execution, unblock obstacles, and maintain cross-team relationships. They define technical vision and build alignment on complex issues while delegating implementation to grow teammates. They're the first called when roadmaps need adjustment.

**Prevalence:** Most common archetype, with roughly one Tech Lead needed per eight engineers.

---

## Architect
**Definition:** Responsible for direction, quality, and approach within a critical technical domain combining deep technical knowledge with user needs and organizational leadership.

**Work & Impact:** Architects maintain intimate understanding of business needs, user goals, and technical constraints. They identify and advocate for effective approaches within their domain, earning organizational authority through consistently good judgment. They remain engaged with the codebase to varying degrees depending on company preference.

---

## Solver
**Definition:** A trusted agent who goes deep into complex problems identified by organizational leadership as critical priorities.

**Work & Impact:** Solvers work on high-risk or unclear problems until resolved, then move to the next priority. They require less organizational negotiation since problems are pre-identified as priorities. Quote: "they generally stop working on problems once they're contained, which can create the feeling of transience."

---

## Right Hand
**Definition:** Operates as a senior organizational leader without managerial responsibilities, extending an executive's attention and authority.

**Work & Impact:** Right Hands attend leadership staff meetings and address problems at the intersection of business, technology, people, and culture. Quote: "pop over to the next fire elsewhere in the organization. The joy of these roles is that you only work on essential problems."

---

## Evaluation & Visibility
Being Staff-level is "the intersection of the role, your behaviors, your impact, and the organization's recognition of all those things"—not merely a title.

This metric (also called "bus factor") measures project vulnerability by identifying critical dependencies on specific individuals, helping assess sustainability if key contributors become unavailable.

This metric tracks how quickly maintainers respond to new issues or pull requests, indicating individual responsiveness and engagement level with community contributions.

## Change Request Closure Ratio
This metric evaluates the proportion of pull requests that are completed versus abandoned, reflecting individual contributors' ability to see work through to completion.

## Change Request Review Duration
This metric measures how long reviewers take to evaluate proposed changes, demonstrating individual efficiency in the code review process.

## Change Request Reviews
This metric quantifies the number of reviews conducted by specific contributors, showing their participation in quality assurance and community guidance.

## Contribution Attribution
This metric documents various forms of contributions beyond code commits, capturing the full scope of individual work including documentation, mentoring, and community support.

All these metrics appear in the CHAOSS knowledge base as officially released measurements for evaluating open source project health and contributor effectiveness.

## Levels and Criteria

PostHog uses a structured leveling system focused on impact rather than hierarchy. According to their handbook, they define levels as follows:

- **Junior**: "contributes to small or function-specific projects"
- **Intermediate**: "owns projects with small to medium impact"
- **Senior**: "owns and drives high-impact projects or a whole product"
- **Staff**: consistently drives large projects affecting the entire company
- **Director/Principal**: operates at the highest levels

## Key Evaluation Approach

The company explicitly states that "Level does not correlate with increased importance, but with impact within PostHog." Importantly, they note this "is not a checklist" and involves "a degree of judgement by the Blitzscale Team."

## Compensation Structure

PostHog uses a transparent formula combining:
1. **Benchmark**: Market-based salary (e.g., $285,000 for San Francisco)
2. **Level modifier**: Applied based on seniority
3. **Step modifier**: Ranges from 0.95 to 1.04

They state they're "open to paying well beyond these ranges for exceptional talent" and explicitly welcome salary negotiations during hiring.

## Quantitative Metrics

The handbook provided contains no mention of specific quantitative performance metrics for evaluation purposes.

input.prompt: Extract Will Larson's framework for measuring engineering organizations. What does he say about individual measurement vs team/org measurement, and what metric categories does he recommend? Verbatim quotes where strong.

content.content:
# Will Larson's Engineering Measurement Framework

## Core Framework: Four Measurement Categories

Larson recommends measuring engineering organizations across four distinct purposes:

1. **Measure to plan**: Track shipped projects by team and their business/product/engineering impacts to support prioritization decisions.

2. **Measure to operate**: Monitor quality metrics including incident frequency, downtime, latency, engineering costs normalized against business metrics, user ratings, and product onboarding conversion rates.

3. **Measure to optimize**: Assess productivity and feedback loops using frameworks like SPACE or Accelerate, or conduct developer productivity surveys.

4. **Measure to inspire and aspire**: Communicate transformational technical investments that enabled previously impossible capabilities.

## Individual vs. Team/Org Measurement

Larson is explicit about this distinction:

**"Measuring individuals rather than teams"** is listed as a major anti-pattern. He argues that software is fundamentally a team activity, noting: *"Writing and operating software is a team activity, and while one engineer might be focused on writing code this sprint, another might be focused on being glue to make it possible for the first engineer to focus."*

His guidance: **"Instead, focus on measuring organization and team-level data. If something seems off, then consider digging into individual data to diagnose, but not to directly evaluate."**

This reflects his conviction that individual metrics mask the collaborative reality of engineering work.

# Measuring Individual Engineering Impact: What the 2024–2026 Literature Actually Says

## The headline tension you are walking into

Every credible source that supplies an individual-level signal also forbids using it for evaluation. That is not a coincidence or a hedge — it is the central, load-bearing claim of the field. Your design has to answer it, not route around it.

The sharpest single formulation, from **Faros AI (Jan 2026)**, on high-AI-adoption teams that completed 21% more tasks and merged 98% more PRs with no measurable delivery improvement: **"Individual velocity was real. System-level impact was not."** ([faros.ai](https://www.faros.ai/blog/lines-of-code-metric-ai-vanity-outcome))

---

## 1. DORA — and three corrections to your premise

**Correction 1: it is five metrics now, not four, and two were renamed.** Current official set at [dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys](https://dora.dev/guides/dora-metrics-four-keys/):

- *Throughput:* **deployment frequency**, **change lead time**, **failed deployment recovery time** (renamed from MTTR/"time to restore" in 2023)
- *Instability:* **change fail rate**, **deployment rework rate** (added 2024 — "the ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production")

Rework rate was added because DORA's researchers found change failure rate "acted as a proxy for the amount of rework a team must perform" ([dora.dev/insights/dora-metrics-history](https://dora.dev/insights/dora-metrics-history/)). **This directly overlaps your thread 6** — DORA has already institutionalized rework as a first-class quality signal, at the team level.

**Correction 2: DORA dropped the elite/high/medium/low clusters in 2025.** Current benchmarks: only 8.5% of teams hit 0–2% change failure rate; the modal band (26%) is 8–16%. Rework rate: 7.3% below 2%, 26.1% at 8–16%.

**Correction 3: DORA's anti-individual language is softer than its reputation.** The four-keys guide does *not* contain an explicit "never use on individuals" sentence. What it says is to apply metrics "at the application or service level" and warns against "setting metrics as a goal." The explicit statement comes from **Nathen Harvey** (DORA lead, Google Cloud) in interviews: *"these metrics are really meant at the level of an application or service"* and *"you have to look at all of them. And you have to have shared accountability for all of them."* His documented misuse case: *"I've heard leaders say every one of my teams has to be an elite performing team by the end of the quarter."* ([multitudes.com interview](https://www.multitudes.com/blog/tech-leader-chats-how-to-use-the-dora-metrics-to-improve-software-team-productivity-with-nathen-harvey))

The strongest citable version of the prohibition is actually **Laura Tacho's**: *"DORA metrics aren't intended to measure the productivity of teams, and certainly never intended to measure the productivity of individuals. They began as a way to benchmark DevOps adoption across the industry."* ([Pragmatic Engineer](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/engineering-productivity))

**AI findings.** 2024 report: AI adoption associated with *decreased* delivery throughput and stability. 2025: AI adoption correlated with worsening on *both* instability metrics (CFR and rework) even as output rose. Practitioner reference for misuse: Bryan Finster, ["How to Misuse & Abuse DORA Metrics"](https://bryanfinster.com/publications/How%20to%20Misuse%20&%20Abuse%20DORA%20Metrics%20-%20DOEJ%20Spring%202022.pdf).

> **Implication for your score.** Do not put DORA metrics in an individual dimension — the deployment pipeline is shared, and Charity Majors' argument kills it outright: *"If it takes the slowest engineer at your company five hours to ship a single line of code, it's going to take the fastest engineer at your company five hours."* The one legitimate individual use, per Tacho, is when *influencing the system is the person's actual job* (platform/DevEx/staff+ roles). Otherwise DORA belongs in your score as **team context that conditions the individual reading**, not as an individual axis.

---

## 2. SPACE — your best friend and your most-cited constraint

The paper: Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Butler, Houck, *ACM Queue*, 2021 ([Microsoft Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-space-of-developer-productivity-theres-more-to-it-than-you-think/)). Five dimensions: **S**atisfaction & well-being, **P**erformance, **A**ctivity, **C**ommunication & collaboration, **E**fficiency & flow. Prescription: at least three dimensions, at least one perceptual measure, metrics spanning individual/team/system levels, never a single metric.

**SPACE is the only peer-reviewed source that explicitly licenses an individual-level metric relevant to your design:**

> "**Code-review velocity captures the speed of reviews; because this can reflect both how quickly an individual completes a review and the constraints of the team, it is both an individual- and a team-level metric.**"

> "a measure or score of the **quality or thoughtfulness** of code reviews is a great qualitative measure of collaboration and communication."

**And it names your two best non-output dimensions in its own myth-busting:**

> *Myth: productivity is only about individual performance.* — "Similar to team sports, success is judged both by a player's personal performance as well as the success of their team. **A developer who optimizes only for their own personal productivity may hurt the productivity of the team.** More team-focused activities such as code reviews, on-call rotations, and developing and managing engineering systems help maintain the quality of the code base."

> *Myth: productivity is only about engineering systems and tools.* — "**Work such as morale building, mentoring, and knowledge sharing are all critical to supporting a productive work environment and yet are often not measured. The 'invisible' work that benefits the overall productivity of the team is just as important as other more commonly-measured dimensions.**"

**But the guardrail is unambiguous:** activity metrics "**should never be used in isolation either to reward or to penalize developers.**" And **Margaret-Anne Storey**: *"I often see companies focusing on metrics like the number of pull requests, which we do not recommend."*

**The best line in this entire body of work** comes from SPACE co-author **Brian Houck** (Microsoft), on PRs per engineer ([DX podcast, Dec 2024](https://getdx.com/podcast/developer-productivity-at-microsoft/)):

> "**It is incredibly poor as an assessment of individual productivity. If you are using it to assess developers, I think it is probably an outright inappropriate metric.** [But] it is really, really powerful and really useful at measuring the health of your system."

*Same metric. Different level. Opposite verdict.*

**The operationalization critique.** Noda & Tacho: *"**SPACE metrics simply don't exist** — it's a misconception to think that it's possible to swap out DORA metrics and use SPACE metrics instead."* And: *"**Just because a metric falls within a SPACE category does not mean it is a 'good' metric or that it will not cause cultural damage.**"* Forsgren herself: *"Once a team has measured or benchmarked itself, **it's inactionable and people feel stuck**."* Houck: *"**SPACE is not a prescriptive framework… That is clearly missing.**"*

Empirically, almost nobody follows the three-dimension rule: a 2025 systematic review of 37–39 studies (arXiv [2507.03156](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.03156)) found ~90% use ≥2 dimensions but **only ~15% use more than three**, with Communication and Activity the least explored.

> **Implication.** SPACE is the framework you should build on, because it is the only one that (a) explicitly names invisible/multiplier work as legitimate, (b) grants code-review velocity individual attribution, and (c) demands multi-dimensionality — which is exactly what you're building. Cite the code-review-velocity sentence verbatim; it is your single strongest license. Then honor the constraint: **no dimension in isolation, and at least one dimension that is not activity.**

---

## 3. DX Core 4 — your hypothesis is half right, and the wrong half is more interesting

Published Dec 10, 2024 by **Abi Noda and Laura Tacho**, with Nicole Forsgren, Michaela Greiler and Thomas Zimmermann iterating ([newsletter.getdx.com](https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/introducing-the-dx-core-4)).

| Dimension | Primary metric |
|---|---|
| **Speed** | Diffs (or PRs) per engineer |
| **Effectiveness** | Developer Experience Index (DXI) — 14 Likert items |
| **Quality** | Change failure rate |
| **Impact** | % of time spent on new capabilities |

Their explicit indictment of the predecessors: *"**DORA** offers prescriptive metrics but has limited scope… **SPACE** provides a framework for defining your own metrics, which is difficult to actually do. **DevEx** focuses on developer experience and self-reported metrics, but it is isolated from the broader concept of productivity."*

**DXI ROI claim:** *"Each one-point gain in DXI score translates to saving **13 minutes per week per developer, equivalent to 10 hours annually**… **the first validated measure of developer productivity that can be directly linked to dollars**."* Built on 40,000+ developers across 800 organizations. (⚠️ LeadDev quotes Noda saying "ten minutes" — cite the 13 and the research page.)

### The stance on individual measurement

**Contrary to your expectation, DX's published framework has NO coaching carve-out. It is stated as an absolute:**

> "**It is critical that this metric is never used at the individual level or tied to performance evaluations.**" — on diffs per engineer

> "**Never measuring metrics like diffs per engineer at the individual level — that's something we stipulate in our framework and build into our product.**" — Abi Noda

> "**Never tie throughput metrics to individual performance.**" / "Measuring how developers spend their time **creates a surveillance culture that undermines trust and creativity**." ([getdx.com/blog/developer-productivity](https://getdx.com/blog/developer-productivity/))

**Reaffirmed in June 2026 by Brian Houck, even after DX built the technical fix:**

> "The criticism of PR throughput is entirely fair at the individual level… DX developed a methodology called **TrueThroughput**, which uses AI to normalize these variations by weighting PRs based on actual complexity. **Yet, even with that kind of normalization in place, the metric is a poor instrument for evaluating any individual developer's contribution. I've argued this myself, and I'd stand by it.**" ([Revisiting the DX Core 4 in the age of AI](https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/revisiting-the-dx-core-4))

**This matters enormously for you:** DX built the exact thing you are building — AI-weighted complexity normalization of PR output — and then explicitly declined to claim it makes individual scoring valid.

**But there is a gap between DX's stated position and its shipped product.** DX's docs describe a **Personal dashboard** giving ICs "metrics around how they are performing" — time allocation, review activity (count and turnaround), PR throughput. And: *"**By default, Dashboard shows individual metrics alongside team metrics.**"* Disabling it is an org-admin toggle. ([docs.getdx.com](https://docs.getdx.com/dashboard/overview/))

**The carve-out you were looking for exists — but at Swarmia and in Laura Tacho's personal writing, not in Core 4.** See threads 4 and 5.

> **Implication.** Do not name your composite score "Impact." Abi Noda has a decade-old, still-live essay explicitly attacking exactly that: a proprietary git-derived composite called "Impact." (Thread 4.) Also: adopt Core 4's **counterbalancing** design — every speed/volume signal paired with an oppositional quality or experience signal — and adopt its **level discipline**: whatever you compute per person, state what it is *for*.

---

## 4. The case against individual metrics — the arguments you must address

### 4a. The single most on-the-nose objection to your project

**Abi Noda's "flawed five" productivity metrics** — commits, lines of code, PR count, velocity points, and **"Impact"** ([getdx.com](https://getdx.com/blog/flawed-productivity-metrics/), originally a GitHub Universe 2019 talk). On the fifth:

> "Here's a definition of this metric from one such vendor: '*Impact attempts to answer the question, "Roughly how much cognitive load did the engineer carry when implementing these changes?" through the severity of edits to the codebase, as compared to repository history.*' Or from another: '*The magnitude of changes to the codebase over a period of time based on whether code is added or changed, the proximity of the edits to one another, and the specific nature of the change on a line-by-line basis.*' **I'm hesitant to call this metric snake oil because I'm sure it is well-intentioned. But anyone who's ever written a line of code knows that there's no legitimacy to this measure.**"

And in the LeadDev version: *"Calling a metric 'Impact' sends a strong signal about how it should be used, particularly by managers. **And this makes it very easy to misuse.**"*

**This is the strongest argument against you, and it is aimed at your exact artifact: a multi-factor, git-derived, per-person composite called an impact score.** You cannot pretend it doesn't exist. Address it head on: name the score something else, publish the formula (Noda's complaint includes opacity — *"it's really difficult to understand because it's calculated using a number of factors"*), and state the intended use explicitly.

### 4b. Empirical: the variance isn't there

**"No Silver Bullets: Why Understanding Software Cycle Time is Messy, Not Magic"** — Flournoy, Lee, Wu, Hicks (Developer Success Lab), arXiv [2503.05040](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.05040). **55,000+ observations, 216 organizations**, Bayesian hierarchical model.

- Individual-level variance SD = **0.645** [0.631, 0.661]; org-level SD = 0.474 — individual variation exceeds organizational variation, and both are dwarfed by residual.
- Effect sizes are tiny: merged PRs within-person −0.0127; collaboration (degree centrality) −0.0023.
- **"Any single observation of cycle time is a very noisy indication of what is typical… most of which are beyond the individual contributor's control."**
- **"one must take great care in comparing cycle-time between individuals even in the same organization, or even against themselves."**
- **"improving software delivery velocity likely requires systems-level thinking rather than individual-focused interventions."**

> **Implication.** If you produce a per-person number, you must produce **uncertainty around it** and a **minimum observation window**. A single quarter of GitHub data on one person is statistically close to noise. Aggregating over ≥2 quarters, showing confidence bands, and refusing to render a score below a data threshold are all defensible engineering responses to this paper — and they turn a fatal objection into a design constraint you've handled.

### 4c. Goodhart, and the mechanism of harm

**Kent Beck** demands every metrics conversation open with Goodhart. His Facebook survey death-spiral is the canonical narrative:

> "Then those scores started cropping up in performance reviews… Directors put pressure on managers for better scores. Managers started negotiating with individual contributors for better survey scores. '**Give me a 5 & I'll make sure you get an "exceeds expectations".**'… Things went from, 'we'd like to know how things are going,' to, '**we know even less about how things are going. But they are definitely going worse because people are now gaming the system.**'"

His operational rules, from the Beck/Orosz McKinsey response ([Part 1](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity), [Part 2](https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-part-2)) — **the single most useful design principle in the entire corpus**:

> "**Avoid perverse incentives by analyzing data at the same level as you collect the data. I can analyze my own data. My team can analyze its own aggregated data.**"

> "**If you choose to create incentives (broadly defined—money, status, promotion, autonomy) around measures, know that you will never again receive accurate data.**"

> "**Red Team any incentives.** What would a clever (you hired them, of course they are clever), motivated person do to make the numbers look better. **How much damage could they cause in the process.**"

> "**The earlier in the cycle you measure, the easier it is to measure. And also the more likely that you introduce unintended consequences.**"

Beck also gave DX a paid grilling ([Feb 2025](https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/developer-productivity-metrics-the)): *"**It's worse than inaccurate, because people degrade the system to produce the number**"* and *"**I would go so far as to say if you just sell the dashboard, that's malpractice.**"*

Beck's surgeon analogy on McKinsey: *"**like if we measured surgeon productivity on what percentage of their time they were cutting with a scalpel or stitching with a needle and we ignored whether the patient got better.**"*

### 4d. The reductionism objection

**Dan North's McKinsey review** ([dannorth.net](https://dannorth.net/blog/mckinsey-review/)) is the most technically detailed takedown, and its most-quoted line is aimed directly at what you're doing:

> "**attempting to measure the individual contribution of a person is like trying to measure the individual contribution of a piston in an engine. The question itself makes no sense.**"

> "**those who contribute less code to solve the same problem, or even who remove unnecessary or redundant code, are often your highest-value developers.**"

> "**Your highest-value developers are 10x by enabling other developers! Often the least useful thing they can be doing is producing code themselves.**"

> "**Applying reductionist thinking and tooling is a category error. 'Better' reductionist tooling is just doubling down on doing the wrong thing with the illusion of rigour.**"

His companion parable, ["The Worst Programmer I Know"](https://dannorth.net/blog/the-worst-programmer/) — Tim Mackinnon, whose story-point score was *literally zero* because he spent every day pairing: **"Tim wasn't delivering software; Tim was delivering a team that was delivering software."**

**Martin Fowler**, ["Cannot Measure Productivity"](https://martinfowler.com/bliki/CannotMeasureProductivity.html) (2003, re-endorsed 2013): we can't measure productivity because **we can't measure output**. *"Any good developer knows that they can code the same stuff with huge variations in lines of code."* True productivity must be based on delivered business value.

**Charity Majors** ([charity.wtf, 2020](https://charity.wtf/2020/07/07/questionable-advice-can-engineering-productivity-be-measured/)):
> "**The team is the irreducible unit of ownership.**"
> "**Some of the hardest and most impactful engineering work will be all but invisible on any set of individual metrics.** You want people to trust that their manager will have their backs and value their contributions appropriately at review time, if they simply act in the team's best interest. **You do not want them to waste time gaming the metrics or courting personal political favor.**"
> "**To the extent you can reduce a job to a set of metrics, that job can be automated away.**"

**Will Larson** ([lethain.com](https://lethain.com/measuring-engineering-organizations/)) — note the concession in the second half, which is the doorway for your work:
> "**Writing and operating software is a team activity, and while one engineer might be focused on writing code this sprint, another might be focused on being glue to make it possible for the first engineer to focus.**"
> "Focus on measuring organization and team-level data. If something seems off, then consider digging into individual data **to diagnose, but not to directly evaluate**."
> Elsewhere: "**Using productivity metrics to measure individuals this way is akin to incident retrospects that identify human error as the root cause.**"

**Gergely Orosz** grants the most ground of anyone in the "against" camp:
> "**There's a wealth of data to look at: but none of it is useful without context.**"
> He accepts individual assessment *by a manager with context*, who can read low commit counts as mentoring rather than laziness. His recommended instrument is a **competency framework tied to career levels**, not metrics.
> His gaming taxonomy: *"Measure effort: create high-effort busywork of dubious value / Measure output: increase the quantity of the output by what's easiest to do / Measure outcomes: aim to beat targets, even if this means taking shortcuts / Measure impact: get creative in reaching this with less effort and output."*
> And: *"**Attributing this impact to individual engineers is also possible, but the more granular you make the attribution, the more this interferes with incentives.**"*

### 4e. Laura Tacho — the most sophisticated position, and the one you should build on

Her essay ["Using Metrics to Measure Individual Developer Performance"](https://lauratacho.com/blog/using-metrics-to-measure-individual-developer-performance) refuses the easy dodge:

> "A lot of research and 'best practice' will tell us that metrics like lines of code, story points completed, or deployment frequency are not appropriate to measure individual performance. This is true… But here's the question we don't talk about enough: '**What data are you going to use to evaluate my performance?**' This is the question that really counts — coming directly from your team members. **There's a better answer than 'best practice says not to use metrics,' which doesn't spark a lot of trust in a fair performance review.**"

> "**Evidence doesn't have to mean activity data.**"

> "**A fast way to reassure your team that you don't understand their job is to pick what they perceive as arbitrary and unfair metrics to measure their performance.**"

> "If I pair with someone and therefore don't commit the code myself, am I penalised? What if I'm working on a design document or coordinating a release? **Responsibilities of developers often go beyond data that can be scraped from GitHub.**"

**Her two explicit exceptions** — this is your "when IS it appropriate" answer:
1. **Seniority-graded.** "It may be perfectly reasonable to look at task-level metrics for a junior engineer, but not for that staff engineer."
2. **Role-matched.** "using team metrics to measure individual performance is generally unfair **unless it's the explicit role of the individual to influence the system performance metrics**."

**And her framing of the legitimate use:** *"Focus on outcomes, not output, **but you might use output metrics like activity from GitHub and JIRA to debug why outcomes were missed**."*

**She also personally rolled out GitPrime to 300+ developers at CloudBees and calls it "a flop":** *"the fundamental idea I could boil down productivity to a handful of metrics which look nice on a dashboard, was – and remains – a myth… **I learned these lessons the hard – and expensive – way.**"* And: *"**In zero cases did those Git Metrics, those activity metrics that you can scrape from an API, tell me something that my team wasn't telling me already.**" / "**People feel very spied on, quite honestly.**"*

### 4f. The GitPrime / Pluralsight Flow cautionary tale — with receipts

$170M acquisition (2019) → rebranded Flow → Vista wrote Pluralsight's equity to zero (May 2024) → sold to Appfire (Feb 2025) → **end of life Dec 31, 2027**.

The verified first-person testimony is devastating and specific:

> "**Gitprime would show a nice dashboard with stack ranked employees based on their git commits.** Besides the obvious effect that it had on cooperation (**you don't want to help another developer lest they go before you in the stack rank**) it had also funny effect on the code we wrote. For example, **replacing old code with new code was penalized as 'code churn', so we had to write something like `if (false) { // old code } // new code`**." — [HN 42040887](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42040887)

> "**The easiest way to shoot up the ranking was to avoid any work where you'd not be instantly coding. Never fix a bug where you need to spend time tracking down the issue, never take on the more complicated pieces of work, never use your time to help out junior team members.**" — [HN 25199703](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=25199703)

> "**almost all the code our 'top coder', per git prime, wrote had to be redone after he got canned. He was copy pasting trash everywhere.**" — [HN 19824747](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19824747)

**The "it depends how you use it" defense, empirically falsified:**
> "I've had **three jobs where Pluralsight Flow was introduced. At two of them, the managers immediately started using the metrics for feedback, performance reviews, employment decisions.**… **the absurd pricing of these tools means that people who approve them have to get some sort of ROI.** Since they don't have a good way to measure productivity, they instead turn to '**Well Jose had less PRs this week…**'" — [HN 42117191](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42117191)

**Bryan Finster** (Walmart DevOps Dojo founder), documenting a GitPrime deployment: teams cherry-picked easy tasks, code-review participation *declined*, staff engineers abandoned mentoring, one team inflated review-comment counts to hit "GitPrime's recommended minimums." Verdict: **"Under no circumstances should this be used."** And his inversion of the cliché: **"'What gets measured gets managed' isn't a recommendation, it's a warning."**

### 4g. The non-tool-specific version of the failure

> "I worked at a major financial supplier whose CEO… **fired hundreds of the 'worst performers' every year based on his spreadsheet. Like clockwork, every year, I saw the most valuable people in every team get fired**, because those were people who had a deep knowledge of the system, and were often diverted from doing 'visible' work by helping less knowledgeable people. They were the ones who trained new hires, who you went to when you couldn't figure out how to debug your problem, who wrote the architecture documentation… **Guess what, none of this stuff showed up in any spreadsheets.**" — [HN 42039648](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42039648)

### 4h. The 10x myth

Origin: Sackman 1968, measuring **individual programmers on isolated coding tasks in a controlled environment** — best vs. *worst*, not best vs. average, and silent on judgment, architecture, mentoring, or communication. Same-person variance across tasks is large. **Google's Project Aristotle** ([re:Work](https://rework.withgoogle.com/en/guides/understanding-team-effectiveness)) explicitly lists "**Individual performance of team members**" among the variables that did **not** predict team effectiveness. *"What really mattered was less about who is on the team, and more about how the team worked together."*

Counterpoint worth holding: PostHog's own handbook says *"we think there is a 10x difference between an average and a top engineer, we pay near the top of market."* They believe in the variance; they just don't measure it with git.

---

## 5. What DOES capture individual impact

### 5a. Code review as leverage — your strongest defensible dimension

- **SPACE** explicitly calls code-review velocity individually attributable (quoted above). This is your license.
- **Google's engineering practices** ([speed.md](https://google.github.io/eng-practices/review/reviewer/speed.html)) set an **individual** SLA: *"**One business day is the maximum time it should take to respond** to a code review request."* Rationale: *"**At Google, we optimize for the speed at which a team of developers can produce a product together, as opposed to optimizing for the speed at which an individual developer can write code.**"* And they separate *individual response* latency from *whole process* latency — *"it's even more important for the individual responses to come quickly than it is for the whole process to happen rapidly."*
- **Sadowski et al., ICSE-SEIP 2018** (9M reviews, Google): median dev authors 3 changes/week, reviews 4, spends **3.2 hrs/week reviewing**. *"the main impetus behind the introduction of code review was to force developers to write code that other developers could understand"* and *"ensuring that more than one person would be familiar with each piece of code, thus **increasing the chances of knowledge staying within the company**."*
- **Bacchelli & Bird, ICSE 2013** (Microsoft): the outcome is not defect-finding. **29% of review comments are code improvements; only 14% are defects.** The quotable line: *"**one of the things that should be happening with code reviews over time is a distribution of knowledge. If you do a code review and did not learn anything about the area and you still do not know anything about the area, then that was not as good code review as it could have been.**"* Their explicit recommendation: *"**Teams should aim to increase the breadth of understanding of developers (if the author of a change is the only expert, she has no potential reviewers).**"*
- **Bosu, Greiler, Bird, MSR 2015** (1.5M Microsoft review comments): *"**reviewers who had reviewed a file before were almost twice more useful (65%–71%) than the first time reviewers (32%–37%)**"* — plateauing around 5 prior reviews. And *"the more files that are in a change, the lower the proportion of comments in the code review that will be of value."*
- **Gergely Orosz:** *"Organizations like this recognise that code reviews take up a good chunk of engineers' time. **Many of these companies will add code reviews as expectations to the developer job competencies, expecting senior engineers to spend a larger chunk of their time reviewing the code of others.**"*

> **Implication.** Review is your best-defended individual axis: it is behavioral, attributable, temporally precise, has a peer-reviewed usefulness proxy (reviewer familiarity), and SPACE names it individual. Measure **response latency** (not process latency), **review depth**, **breadth of files reviewed outside your own ownership**, and **reviews of external contributors** separately. ### 5e. Bus factor / knowledge concentration — with a serious complication

**Avelino, Passos, Hora, Valente, "A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors," ICPC 2016** ([arXiv 1604.06766](https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.06766), [tool](https://github.com/aserg-ufmg/Truck-Factor)) — the method is fully specified and reproducible from git alone:

- **DOA(md, fp) = 3.293 + 1.098·FA + 0.164·DL − 0.321·ln(1 + AC)** where FA = created the file (1/0), DL = that dev's changes, AC = everyone else's changes.
- Author iff normalized DOA > **0.75** and absolute DOA ≥ **3.293**. TF = greedily remove top authors until file coverage drops below **50%**.
- Findings across 133 systems: **65% have TF ≤ 2; 34% have TF = 1.** Follow-up on 1,932 projects: **57% have TF = 1, 25% TF = 2.**
- Their own mitigation finding: **"documentation is the most effective development practice to overcome a truck factor event."**

**CHAOSS's version** is "Contributor Absence Factor" — *"the smallest number of contributors responsible for 50% of total contributions"* (renamed from Bus Factor). The continuous alternative, better for scoring, is the **Development Distribution Score**: `DDS = 1 − (top committer's commits / total commits)`, implemented in [ecosyste.ms](https://github.com/ecosyste-ms/commits). Median across OSS is **0.304** — most projects have one developer writing ~70% of commits.

**⚠️ The complication that should change your design: concentration has two opposite signs.**

**Bird, Nagappan, Murphy, Gall, Devanbu, "Don't Touch My Code!" ESEC/FSE 2011** (Windows Vista and 7):
> "**The number of minor contributors has a strong positive relationship with both pre- and post-release failures** even when controlling for size, churn, and complexity."
> "**Higher levels of ownership for the top contributor to a component results in fewer failures.**"

So: high concentration = **lower defect risk**, **higher continuity risk**. The bus-factor literature only measures the second. **Adam Tornhill's resolution is the defensible one:** the risk signal is concentration **×** hotspot **×** poor code health, not concentration alone. His "Knowledge Island in Complex Hotspot" is the flagged case; a knowledge island in *healthy* code is explicitly *"lower risk."*

**⚠️ Two more caveats on the method:** the DOA constants come from Fritz et al., ICSE 2010, fitted on **246 ratings from 7 developers, R² = 0.25** — every subsequent paper reuses them unchanged. And there is **no time decay**: JetBrains' 269-engineer survey found a practitioner-estimated knowledge **half-life of ~4 months**, and that the baseline algorithm "predicted a key developer who is not active anymore (last commit > 1.5 years ago)." They also found practitioners believe **<20%** of files can be abandoned before trouble, not Avelino's 50%.

**JetBrains' pitfall list, which applies directly to you:** *"A key engineer may feel irreplaceable, which may negatively impact their relationship with their employer"* / *"Those not listed as key engineers may feel underestimated"* / *"**the tool should be used on an opt-in basis per team.**"*

### 5f. Blast radius / criticality of code touched

**This is your best-supported weighting principle, and it has a 2005 proof.**

**Nagappan & Ball, ICSE 2005** ([MSR](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/use-of-relative-code-churn-measures-to-predict-system-defect-density/)), on 2,465 Windows Server 2003 binaries:

| Model | R² |
|---|---|
| **Absolute** churn measures | **0.052** |
| Absolute + PCA | 0.026 |
| **Relative** churn measures (all ratios) | **0.811** |

> "**while absolute measures of code churn are poor predictors of defect density, our set of relative measures of code churn is highly predictive**… able to discriminate between fault and not fault-prone binaries with an accuracy of **89.0 percent**."

**The whole finding is that raw change volume is worthless and volume normalized by what it touches is strong.** That is your weighting argument, established twenty years ago on a real system.

**Adam Tornhill's hotspots** (change frequency × complexity):
> "**all code isn't equal.** …it's a huge difference to increase a simple version number in a single-line file compared to correcting a bug in a file with 5,000 lines of C++ with tricky, nested conditional logic."
> "the prioritized Hotspots only make up **2–3% of the total code size**. Yet there's a disproportional amount of development activity in that small part with **11–16% of all commits**… responsible for **25–70% of all reported and resolved defects**."
> "**most code isn't as important as we'd like to think.**"

Peer-reviewed backing: **Tornhill & Borg, "Code Red," TechDebt 2022** ([arXiv 2203.04374](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04374)), 39 proprietary codebases / 30,737 files: *"**Low quality code contains 15 times more defects**"* / *"resolving issues in low quality code takes on average **124% more time**"* / *"**9 times longer maximum cycle times.**"*

**How to combine heterogeneous criticality signals into a bounded score — Rob Pike's OpenSSF Criticality Score formula** ([spec PDF](https://github.com/ossf/criticality_score/blob/main/Quantifying_criticality_algorithm.pdf)):

> C = (1/Σαᵢ) · Σ αᵢ · log(1+Sᵢ) / log(1 + max(Sᵢ, Tᵢ))

His rationale is exactly the problem you have: *"a naive weighted sum is unbounded… **A package with 10,000 dependents is surely more important than a package with only 1,000, but arguably not ten times more.**"* Log-scale, clamp at a per-signal threshold, weight, normalize to [0,1]. Their heaviest weights are **fan-in** and **contributor breadth**; staleness *reduces* criticality. **Steal this formula.**

Architectural version: **MacCormack, Baldwin & Rusnak's propagation cost** — *"the proportion of elements that could be affected, on average, when a change is made to one element."* Their warning: *"detecting a core-periphery structure **cannot be achieved solely by examining the direct dependencies**, but requires an assessment of all potential paths through which dependencies propagate."* 80% of 1,286 releases have a core-periphery structure, with cores 12–64% of the system.

Every published ladder encodes scope, not output. From [progression.fyi](https://progression.fyi/) (75 frameworks):

**Dropbox**: *"Our career growth framework is anchored on results, aka business impact, which is a function of our **scope of impact**."* IC1 "defined tasks" → IC3 "projects in service of quarterly goals on the team" → IC5 "**multi-year, multi-team**" → IC7 "**company-wide**." ## 6. Code churn / rework rate

**Origin: GitPrime's taxonomy**, recovered verbatim from the Internet Archive (their site is dead):

> **Churn** — "Code which was thrown away shortly after being written (**less than 3 weeks old**)"
> **New Work** — "Brand new code that does not replace other code."
> **Legacy Refactor** — "Code that updates or edits old code."
> **Help Others** — "Code where a developer modifies **someone else's** recent work (less than 3 weeks old)"
> **Efficiency** — "The percentage of all contributed code which is productive work."

Note the ownership boundary that gets lost in every repackaging: **churn is your own recent code; help-others is someone else's recent code.** Same 21-day window, different author.

**The baseline you remembered, with its primary source** — Travis Kimmel, "3 Misconceptions about Code Churn," GitPrime:
> "**In benchmarking the code contribution patterns of over 85,000 software engineers… Code Churn levels most frequently run between 13-30% of all code committed (i.e., 70-87% Efficiency), where a typical team can expect to operate in the neighborhood of 75% Efficiency.**"
> "**Myth #1: Code Churn is 'bad.' Reality: Code Churn is neither good nor bad — it's a useful signal.**"
> "**Code Churn can be lumpy. A healthy project may have elevated Churn at the beginning of a project and lower Churn towards the end.**"

**⚠️ The caveats — from GitPrime's own blog, and they're brutal.** Ben Thompson's "6 Causes of Code Churn" lists **four of six causes as organizational or benign** (unclear requirements, indecisive stakeholder, polishing via code review, under-engagement/burnout), and gives baselines **2–6× the "healthy" band** for legitimate work:
> "**Difficult problem** — It would not be uncommon for churn rates to **exceed 60-80%**."
> "**Prototyping** — you would expect them to explore multiple implementation paths… churn rates in the **60-80% range may not be unusual**."

**And Kimmel himself disavowed individual scoring:**
> "**Our general approach here has not been so much to focus on the individual engineer. We don't want people obsessing about this stuff.**… It's a thing that kind of lends itself to abuse. **You don't want to infantilize your workforce.**"

*The founder disavowed individual gamification; the acquirer shipped leaderboards.*

**The fatal technical critique — Bill Harding (GitClear founder):**
> "**Churn only exists relative to a developer's commit habits.** That is, if Alice makes one commit per day, she will appear to have low churn since all of her work was lumped together. If Bob makes 10 commits that end up accomplishing the exact same work, he's going to appear to have a problem with churn. **Our belief is that the work style of Bob and Alice are both fine.**"

**⚠️ Also note: window definitions are not standardized.** GitPrime = 21 days. GitClear = 14 days. DORA's rework rate is deployment-based, not line-based. Pick one and publish it.

**The AI-era shift (GitClear, 211M changed lines, Jan 2020 – Dec 2024):** churn rose **3.1% → 5.7%**; refactoring collapsed from **25% of changed lines (2021) to under 10% (2024)**; copy-pasted lines rose **8.3% → 12.3%**, crossing above moved/refactored code for the first time; duplicated blocks up **8×** in 2024.

**Revert rate as a GitHub-observable signal:** baselines are roughly **1.6% of commits reverted**, 0.7% causing CI failures. ⚠️ Heavily confounded by team convention — teams that `git revert` produce signal; teams that fix-forward or force-push produce none. Not comparable across orgs.

**⭐ Tornhill's stance is your strongest citation in this whole thread** (SE Radio 554):
> "[Managers ask] '**can you go into our organization and can you rank all of my programmers so I know who to reward and who to fire?**' **I always said no to that.**"
> "**If you need to have that outside information as a manager, you are probably not as close to your team as you should be.**"
> "**What we did as a company with CodeScene was that we did a formal statement that we are never going to evaluate individuals. What we do is, we could evaluate the team.**"

*The person who built the most sophisticated commercially available git-history analysis has a written company policy against pointing it at people.*

> **Implication.** Use churn — but (a) **relative, never absolute** (Nagappan & Ball: R² 0.811 vs 0.052); (b) **normalize for commit granularity**, or Harding's objection lands; (c) **exempt or flag** prototyping/greenfield/exploratory contexts where 60–80% is normal; (d) prefer **DORA's deployment rework rate** or PR revert rate as the harder signal, and (e) present it as **the canary Thompson called it**, not a score component with a threshold.

**3. The variance isn't there.** 55,000 observations, 216 orgs: individual-level SD 0.645, effect sizes ~0.01, *"any single observation… is a very noisy indication of what is typical."* **Response:** confidence intervals, minimum observation windows, and refusing to render below a data threshold.

**4. It has been tried, at scale, and it went badly in documented, specific ways.** Engineers wrote `if (false) { // old code }` to defeat churn detection; stopped helping teammates to protect their stack rank; a "top coder" whose code all had to be rewritten. Laura Tacho — now co-author of Core 4 — rolled it out to 300+ developers and calls it *"a flop."* Bryan Finster documented code-review participation *declining* and staff engineers abandoning mentoring. Two of three employers began using it for employment decisions immediately. **Response:** Beck's red-team exercise — for every dimension, write down what a clever, motivated person does to game it, and how much damage that causes.

**5. Google already ran your experiment and nothing happened.** Lewis, Lin, Sadowski, Zhu, Ou, Whitehead, ICSE 2013: *"We deployed a bug prediction algorithm across Google, and **found no identifiable change in developer behavior.**"* Their diagnosis is a design spec: it must be **actionable** (*"the development team should be able to take clear steps that will result in the area no longer being flagged"*); it must offer a **path to a clean bill of health**, not *"a revolving door of problems, which is likely very disheartening"*; and it must be **obviously reasoned** — *"the burden of proof is always on the tool to precisely elucidate why it has come to the conclusion it has."* Notably, the simple explainable baseline **beat** the sophisticated algorithm in developer judgment.

**Bonus, and it's the one people skip:** Larson's **preening** — *"Many companies conflate high-visibility and high-impact so strongly that they can't distinguish between preening and impact."* A GitHub-derived score measures visibility. You need an explicit answer for why yours isn't a preening detector.

### The strongest arguments FOR

- **Tacho's question is unanswered by the refuseniks:** *"What data are you going to use to evaluate my performance?"* — *"There's a better answer than 'best practice says not to use metrics,' which doesn't spark a lot of trust in a fair performance review."*
- **Reilly's own ask:** glue work *"needs to be tracked whatever way the team tracks its other work."* Making it legible is her explicit recommendation.
- **The bias argument.** NCWIT: 30+ years of research shows stereotypes fill the gap *"when performance information is lacking or ambiguous."* Ambiguous criteria and missing evidence are what bias runs on. Reilly's 48%/44% statistics say glue work is disproportionately done by women — and disproportionately invisible. **A structured evidence base that surfaces review, mentoring and community work is a plausible bias reducer, and that is the affirmative case for your project.**
- **SPACE explicitly licenses code-review velocity as individual**, and explicitly names *"morale building, mentoring, and knowledge sharing"* as invisible work that *"is just as important as other more commonly-measured dimensions."*
- **Nagappan & Ball proved the normalization principle** twenty years ago: absolute volume R²=0.05, relative R²=0.81.

## Concrete design implications, consolidated

1. **Don't call it "Impact."** Noda's essay makes that name a liability. Consider framing it as a *contribution profile* or *evidence summary* rather than a score.
2. **Publish the formula.** Opacity is half of the "Impact metric" critique and the entirety of LinearB's attack on the DXI (*"Black box proprietary formula makes it impossible to know what actions will improve it"*).
3. **Normalize everything.** Nagappan & Ball. Use Pike's criticality formula shape — log-scale each signal, clamp at a per-signal threshold, weight, normalize to [0,1] — so no single signal can run away.
4. **Weight by blast radius**, computed via propagation/fan-in over the *transitive* dependency closure, not direct edges (MacCormack). Hotspots are 2–3% of code and 25–70% of defects.
5. **Profile shapes, not one ranked list.** Use Larson's archetypes as the interpretive frame — the same GitHub footprint means opposite things for a Solver and a Tech Lead. This is your answer to "senior engineers look bad on activity metrics."
6. **Make review a first-class dimension**: individual response latency (not process latency), review breadth outside owned files, external-contributor review as a separate axis.
7. **Handle churn carefully**: relative only, normalized for commit granularity, context-exempted for greenfield/prototyping, presented as a canary.
8. **Treat knowledge concentration as two-signed**: flag concentration × hotspot × poor health (Tornhill), not concentration alone (Bird et al.). Add time decay — practitioners estimate a ~4-month knowledge half-life.
9. **Ship uncertainty**: confidence bands, minimum windows, refusal below a data threshold.
10. **Follow Beck's level-matching rule and Swarmia's architecture**: the IC sees their own data; no side-by-side ranking; no manager-only view.
11. **Meet Google's ICSE 2013 bar**: actionable, with a reachable clean state, and with the reasoning surfaced for every flag.
12. **Red-team every dimension** and publish the gaming analysis alongside the metric.
13. **For PostHog specifically**, cite their own handbook — *"some people with low PR output are very valuable… heavy support load can impact output"* — as the justification for the community/support dimension.

## Corrections to premises in the brief

- **DORA is five metrics, not four**, with two renamed (failed deployment recovery time; deployment rework rate added 2024). The elite/high/medium/low tiers were dropped in 2025.
- **DX Core 4 has no coaching carve-out** — the published prohibition is absolute. The carve-out you expected exists at **Swarmia** (product architecture) and in **Laura Tacho's personal writing** (seniority-graded and role-matched exceptions).
- **Laura Tacho was CTO at DX 2023–2026 and is now Senior Principal Technologist, Developer Experience, at AWS.** Don't describe her as DX's current CTO in 2026-dated material.
- **The Development Distribution Score is from the OpenSustain.tech report** (Augspurger, Malliaraki, Hopkins), implemented in ecosyste.ms — not from Yegor Bugayenko.
- **CHAOSS renamed "Bus Factor" to "Contributor Absence Factor."**
- **Beck & Orosz is a two-part series**, not three or four (four artifacts because it cross-published on both newsletters).
- **The McKinsey article's authors are Gnanasambandam, Harrysson, Hussin, Keovichit and Srivastava** — Wenjie Wu is not an author. It cites DORA and SPACE but never cites Nicole Forsgren or any coauthor, which is North's sharpest charge.
- **Code Climate Velocity did not shut down** — only its free tier ("Velocity for Teams," data deleted March 2024). Pluralsight/Appfire Flow's EOL is **Dec 31, 2027**, announced but not yet executed.
- **No Kent Beck writing about GitPrime by name exists.** The named-authority attacks on GitPrime are Finster, Harding, and Tacho's own CloudBees account.
- **The "AI slop / DoS on human attention" lines are third-party commentary, not GitHub's Octoverse wording.** Octoverse 2024 said the opposite: *"we did not see a rise in rejected pull requests."*
- **⚠️ Verify independently before publishing:** the Musk/lines-of-code Twitter evaluation story (only vendor-blog sourcing obtained), and the DXI "10 vs 13 minutes" discrepancy (cite 13, from DX's research page).
